“Hu bowed and touched his head to the ground; may the Son of Heaven live ten thousand years!”

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Instructor: Those who write on this topic suffer from stale and commonplace language. This essay is fresh, precise, and apt; one never tires of reading it aloud. Moreover, its loyal devotion overflows beyond the words. What doubt could there be about recommending it highly?

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: Clear in reasoning and fluent in expression; this is no careless composition.

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: It captures the intention of wishing the ruler long life.

In his relations with his ruler, a great minister receives commands with reverence and repays imperial favor with wishes for long life. To feel gratitude for favor and seek to repay it is the duty of a subject. A great minister receives commands reverently, and, in repaying favor, offers wishes for longevity. How profound is his loyal devotion! In former times, King Xuan commanded Duke Mu of Shao to pacify the Huai Yi, and the poet praised him. At this point, it is as though the poet said: “When a ruler employs his ministers, there are ceremonies for rewarding achievement; when a minister loves his ruler, there is sincerity in repaying his beneficence. How did Shao Hu conduct himself toward the king? The king, mindful of his achievements in the Jiang and Han regions, bestowed abundant gifts and favor, displaying the glory and excellence of his lineage. His formal investiture could indeed be called magnificent. Hu, receiving favor bestowed from Heaven, bowed low…”

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
登嘉若弗克勝幸希世之遭逢而稽首拜受罔
敢或忽雖命在文考之庭而感激之意周旋於
盤辟之間蓋儼天威於咫尺者矣雖身在岐周
之廟而翼畏之容踧踖於傴僂之際固仰清穆
於瞻承者矣夫稽首受命一敬之不容巳也然
其祝願效忠之私殆有出於常情之外者迺曰
爲元后作民父母天子於今日固尊榮矣其必
自天佑之而壽考萬年長守貴焉以一人玉食
萬方天子於今日固茀祿矣其必天保定爾而
===
萬壽無疆長守富焉履位于乾保大于豐秩祜
申錫之休永爲天地山川之主也凝命於鼎享
治於泰純嘏有常之慶永爲華夏蠻貊之宗也
是人君所可願欲者莫大於此必如是吾報答
之心或少盡矣噫于以見召公敬王之禮焉于
以見召公報王之義焉世臣忠愛至是哉雖然
矢文德洽四國則所以養壽命之源置天下仁
壽之域公之忠愛尤深遠也故曰太上壽德其
次壽名天子萬年之頌文德四國之洽其壽德
punctuated: 登嘉，若弗克勝，幸希世之遭逢，而稽首拜受，罔敢或忽。雖命在文考之庭，而感激之意周旋於盤辟之間，蓋儼天威於咫尺者矣；雖身在岐周之廟，而翼畏之容踧踖於傴僂之際，固仰清穆於瞻承者矣。夫稽首受命，一敬之不容巳也。然其祝願效忠之私，殆有出於常情之外者，迺曰：「爲元后，作民父母，天子於今日固尊榮矣，其必自天佑之，而壽考萬年，長守貴焉；以一人玉食萬方，天子於今日固茀祿矣，其必天保定爾，而萬壽無疆，長守富焉。履位于乾，保大于豐，秩祜申錫之休，永爲天地山川之主也；凝命於鼎，享治於泰，純嘏有常之慶，永爲華夏蠻貊之宗也。是人君所可願欲者，莫大於此。必如是，吾報答之心或少盡矣。」噫！于以見召公敬王之禮焉，于以見召公報王之義焉。世臣忠愛至是哉！雖然，矢文德，洽四國，則所以養壽命之源，置天下仁壽之域，公之忠愛尤深遠也。故曰：「太上壽德，其次壽名。」天子萬年之頌，文德四國之洽，其壽德
translation_en:
…accepting the gracious gifts as though unable to bear their weight, he rejoiced in this encounter so rarely granted in any age. He bowed his head to the ground and reverently received them, daring no negligence. Although the command was bestowed in the court of the king’s illustrious deceased father, his gratitude found expression in his every ceremonial turn and bow: he stood in awe of Heaven’s majesty so close at hand. Although he stood in the ancestral temple at Qizhou, his reverent fear appeared in his cautious movements and bent posture: as he looked up and received the command, he indeed revered the king’s pure and solemn presence. Bowing his head to receive the command was an expression of reverence that could not be restrained. Yet his inward wish to offer blessings and demonstrate loyalty went, perhaps, beyond ordinary feeling. Thus he said:
“As supreme sovereign and father and mother to the people, the Son of Heaven assuredly enjoys honor and glory today. May Heaven surely assist him, granting him ten thousand years of long life, so that he may preserve his exalted station forever. As the One Man, enjoying the finest food from the myriad regions, the Son of Heaven assuredly possesses abundant blessings today. May Heaven surely protect and establish you, granting you boundless longevity, so that you may preserve your wealth forever. Taking his position in Qian, ‘The Creative,’ and preserving his greatness in Feng, ‘Abundance,’ may he enjoy the favor of great blessings bestowed anew, forever presiding over the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, mountains and rivers. Securing his mandate in Ding, ‘The Cauldron,’ and enjoying good government in Tai, ‘Peace,’ may he rejoice in enduring, ample blessings, forever remaining the acknowledged sovereign of the Huaxia people and the Man and Mo peoples. Nothing that a ruler might wish for exceeds this. Only if it comes to pass might my desire to repay his favor be fulfilled in some small measure.”
Ah! Here we see the ritual propriety with which the Duke of Shao honored his king; here we see the righteousness with which he repaid his king. Could the loyalty and affection of a hereditary minister reach such a height! Yet his pledge to spread civil virtue throughout the four quarters nourished the very source of longevity and brought all under Heaven into a realm of benevolence and long life. In this, the duke’s loyalty and affection were still more profound and far-reaching. Thus it is said: “Highest is to give lasting life to virtue; next is to give lasting life to one’s name.” His praise wishing the Son of Heaven ten thousand years, and the extension of civil virtue throughout the four quarters—was this not giving lasting life to virtue…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
壽天下乎頌而無諂召虎以之嗚呼周家有道
之長宣王壽德之應可徵矣
受小球大球爲下國綴旒何天之休不競
不絿不剛不柔敷政優優百祿是遒受
小共大共爲下國駿厖何天之龍敷奏
其勇不震不動不戁不竦百祿是總
蕭應韶
同考試官敎諭江批成湯昭受天命全在敬
上此作最得本旨且收裾簡當無浮泛冗長之病
是固有醞藉者錄以式多士
考試官敎諭黃批格語峻整佳士也
考試官學正林批簡而文
詩人兩著聖人受命之迹而必本其所自也夫
天人之際判矣而其機恒相感也則夫成湯有
此善政武功天其能舍諸此商人於禘祭之頌
而頌之意謂惟我成湯懋敬格天而天旣命之
以式圍矣抑何以見之天子統萬方而居則凡
天下之玉帛要皆惟皇之所錫也是故我商大
punctuated:
壽天下乎？頌而無諂，召虎以之。嗚呼！周家有道之長，宣王壽德之應可徵矣。

「受小球大球，爲下國綴旒，何天之休。不競不絿，不剛不柔，敷政優優，百祿是遒。受小共大共，爲下國駿厖，何天之龍。敷奏其勇，不震不動，不戁不竦，百祿是總。」

蕭應韶

同考試官敎諭江批：「成湯昭受天命，全在敬上。此作最得本旨，且收裾簡當，無浮泛冗長之病，是固有醞藉者，錄以式多士。」

考試官敎諭黃批：「格語峻整，佳士也。」

考試官學正林批：「簡而文。」

詩人兩著聖人受命之迹，而必本其所自也。夫天人之際判矣，而其機恒相感也。則夫成湯有此善政武功，天其能舍諸？此商人於禘祭之頌而頌之，意謂惟我成湯懋敬格天，而天旣命之以式圍矣。抑何以見之？天子統萬方而居，則凡天下之玉帛，要皆惟皇之所錫也。是故我商大
translation_en:
…and bring longevity to all under Heaven? Song Hu offered praise without flattery. Ah! The long endurance of the Zhou house under the Way bears witness to the response evoked by King Xuan’s virtue of longevity.

“He received the small jade spheres and the large jade spheres, serving as the standard to which the subordinate states were attached, bearing Heaven’s favor. Neither contentious nor impetuous, neither hard nor soft, he spread his government with generous ease, and the hundred blessings converged upon him. He received the small jade disks and the large jade disks, serving as the mighty protector of the subordinate states, bearing Heaven’s bounty. He displayed and exerted his valor, neither trembling nor wavering, neither fearful nor alarmed, and the hundred blessings gathered upon him.”

Xiao Yingshao

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Instructor: “Cheng Tang’s illustrious reception of Heaven’s mandate rested entirely on reverence for what is above. This composition captures the fundamental meaning particularly well. Its closing [?] is also concise and fitting, free of vagueness and excessive length. It certainly possesses depth and restraint; it is recorded here as a model for the candidates.”

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: “The structure and language are elevated and orderly. An excellent scholar.”

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: “Concise yet elegant.”

The poet twice makes manifest the evidence of the sage’s reception of the mandate, invariably tracing it to its source. Heaven and humanity occupy distinct realms, yet their workings constantly respond to one another. Given Cheng Tang’s excellent government and military achievements, could Heaven possibly pass him over? Thus the people of Shang praised him in their hymn for the di sacrifice. Their meaning was this: our Cheng Tang earnestly cultivated reverence and thereby reached Heaven, and Heaven had already commanded him to govern the realm. But how is this demonstrated? The Son of Heaven occupies his position as ruler of the myriad regions; all the jade and silk throughout the world are, in essence, bestowed by August Heaven. Thus, in our Shang, the large…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
小之球咸於湯受焉則有以為下國之綴旒而
何天之休矣然天德無私親其所以得此者匪
私干之也蓋帝王之政所貴者中而天命去留
之機恒於此乎繫焉今我湯以日躋之敬而敷
於政也於其競狃而相為倚伏焉於其剛柔而
相為運用焉寬裕而不拘中行而無迹則凝命
迓休之道其在此也百祿不是遒乎天子以四
海為家則凡庶邦之財賦要皆惟辟之玉食也
是故我商大小之共咸於湯受焉則有以為下
===
國之駿厖而何天之龍矣然天心無常享其所
以得此者匪倖致之也蓋王者之師存乎仁義
而天命予奪之會每於此乎定焉今我湯以日
躋之敬而敷奏其勇也於其仁以育物而震動
不形焉於其義以剛中而戅竦不作焉德威竝
著天下歸心則祈天永命之道其在此也百祿
不是總乎夫成湯以敬受命之迹如此則知天
人之相與蓋有會逢其適者矣稽古溫恭祇台
後此敬止敬勝治化洽而祚運長率是道也覲
punctuated: 小之球，咸於湯受焉，則有以為下國之綴旒，而何天之休矣。然天德無私親，其所以得此者，匪私干之也。蓋帝王之政，所貴者中，而天命去留之機，恒於此乎繫焉。今我湯以日躋之敬而敷於政也，於其競狃而相為倚伏焉，於其剛柔而相為運用焉。寬裕而不拘，中行而無迹，則凝命迓休之道，其在此也。百祿不是遒乎？天子以四海為家，則凡庶邦之財賦，要皆惟辟之玉食也。是故我商大小之共，咸於湯受焉，則有以為下國之駿厖，而何天之龍矣。然天心無常享，其所以得此者，匪倖致之也。蓋王者之師存乎仁義，而天命予奪之會，每於此乎定焉。今我湯以日躋之敬而敷奏其勇也，於其仁以育物而震動不形焉，於其義以剛中而戅竦不作焉。德威竝著，天下歸心，則祈天永命之道，其在此也。百祿不是總乎？夫成湯以敬受命之迹如此，則知天人之相與，蓋有會逢其適者矣。稽古溫恭，祇台；後此敬止，敬勝，治化洽而祚運長，率是道也。覲
translation_en: …the small jade tokens were all received by Tang; thus he could serve as the rallying point of the lesser states and bear Heaven’s blessings. Yet Heaven’s virtue shows no private partiality: he obtained these blessings without seeking them for his own advantage. For what is prized in the government of emperors and kings is the mean, and the crucial issue of whether Heaven’s Mandate departs or remains is always bound up with this. Now our Tang, with reverence that advanced daily, extended it to his government. In contention and complacency [?], he allowed each to counterbalance the other; in firmness and gentleness, he employed each in conjunction with the other. Generous and unconfined, he followed the mean without leaving any trace of effort. Here lay the way to secure the Mandate and welcome blessings. Did not the hundred blessings therefore converge upon him? The Son of Heaven takes all within the Four Seas as his household; thus the wealth and revenues of the many states are, in essence, all provisions for the sovereign’s sumptuous meals. Accordingly, the offerings of our Shang’s great and small states were all received by Tang; thus he could become the mighty protector of the lesser states and bear Heaven’s favor. Yet Heaven’s heart does not perpetually accept the same ruler’s offerings: he obtained this favor without relying on chance. For the armies of a true king rest upon benevolence and righteousness, and the decisive occasion for Heaven to grant or withdraw its Mandate is always determined here. Now our Tang, with reverence that advanced daily, displayed and brought to fruition his valor. Through benevolence he nurtured all beings, without any manifestation of terrifying force; through righteousness he was firm and centered, without rashness or alarm [?]. Virtue and majesty shone forth together, and the hearts of all under Heaven turned to him. Here lay the way to pray to Heaven for an enduring Mandate. Were not the hundred blessings therefore gathered together? Such were the manifestations of Cheng Tang’s receiving the Mandate through reverence. We may therefore know that, in the mutual relations of Heaven and humanity, there are encounters that occur at precisely the fitting moment. Examining antiquity, we find warmth and respect, and the injunction, “Be reverent toward me”; thereafter, abiding in reverence and allowing reverence to prevail [?], rulers brought their transforming governance everywhere and prolonged their dynastic fortunes, all by following this way. Behold…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
湯之盤銘自警昧爽日新則其優優之政不殺
之武見於建中綏猷推亡固存者厥有遺烈矣
況當時之大畏小懷乎故曰大德者必受命
春秋
蔡侯鄭伯會于鄧桓公二年
陳試
同考試官教諭張批入春秋為楚懼者寔自
三國始聖人傷之其慮遠矣此篇檃括傳意而蔚
然成章宜錄以式
===
考試官教諭黃批得聖人強本治內之旨
考試官學正林批順暢可誦經義之優者
春秋紀諸侯講好而著其懼外之失焉此三國
懼楚而忘其所以自治者故春秋傷之如此且
蔡鄭曷為乎會鄧也蓋自黍離降而包茅之貢
絕姬轍東而乘廣之焰熾楚為中國患也駸駸
乎日以張矣三國皆鄰於楚者乃即于鄧會焉
推戒心以要言援脩睦以相結凡以為楚也君
子謂諸侯于是乎始懼楚矣夫楚之可懼者勢
punctuated:
湯之盤銘，自警昧爽，日新，則其優優之政、不殺之武，見於建中綏猷、推亡固存者，厥有遺烈矣。況當時之大畏小懷乎？故曰：「大德者必受命。」

春秋
蔡侯、鄭伯會于鄧。桓公二年。
陳試

同考試官教諭張批：「入春秋，為楚懼者，寔自三國始。聖人傷之，其慮遠矣。此篇檃括傳意，而蔚然成章，宜錄以式。」
考試官教諭黃批：「得聖人強本治內之旨。」
考試官學正林批：「順暢可誦，經義之優者。」

春秋紀諸侯講好，而著其懼外之失焉。此三國懼楚，而忘其所以自治者，故春秋傷之如此。且蔡、鄭曷為乎會鄧也？蓋自黍離降而包茅之貢絕，姬轍東而乘廣之焰熾，楚為中國患也，駸駸乎日以張矣。三國皆鄰於楚者，乃即于鄧會焉，推戒心以要言，援脩睦以相結，凡以為楚也。君子謂諸侯于是乎始懼楚矣。夫楚之可懼者，勢
translation_en:
…Tang’s inscription on his basin: he admonished himself at daybreak to renew himself daily. His generous government and his martial power that did not kill, manifested in establishing the mean and securing the Way, overthrowing doomed states and strengthening those that endured, left achievements for posterity. How much more, then, did the great states of his own time fear him and the small cherish him! Thus it is said: “One of great virtue will surely receive the Mandate.”

Spring and Autumn Annals
“The Marquis of Cai and the Earl of Zheng met at Deng.” Second year of Duke Huan.
Chen Shi

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “In the Spring and Autumn period, fear of Chu indeed began with these three states. The Sage lamented this; his concern reached far into the future. This essay recasts the meaning of the Commentary into a richly accomplished composition. It should be recorded as a model.”
Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: “It grasps the Sage’s intent of strengthening the foundations and governing internally.”
Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: “Fluent and pleasing to recite; an excellent exposition of the Classic.”

The Spring and Autumn Annals records the feudal lords cultivating friendly relations, thereby exposing their error in fearing an external power. These three states feared Chu but forgot the means of governing themselves; hence the Annals’ lament over them. Why, then, did Cai and Zheng meet at Deng? Since ‘Millet Separation’ was relegated to the Airs and the tribute of bundled mao grass ceased, since the carriage tracks of the house of Ji turned eastward and the might of Chu’s war chariots blazed forth, the danger Chu posed to the central states had grown steadily greater each day. All three states bordered Chu, and so they assembled at Deng. They gave expression to their apprehensions through solemn pledges and bound themselves together by cultivating amity—all on account of Chu. The gentleman says that it was at this point that the feudal lords began to fear Chu. Now, what made Chu fearsome was its power…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
也而其可恃以無恐者不有自治之道乎使能
任賢明政而樹德以奠邦輯眾善鄰而協謀以
禦侮則人和固於城郭忠信堅於甲胄荆楚雖
大何懼焉而乃好會徒煩訂謨罔協不虞弗戒
空懷剥牀之憂豈以楚地五千里其大不可敵
也不思天下莫大於理不循天理而以地之大
小分勝負可乎先事弗備徒懾門庭之寇抑以
帶甲數十萬其强不可敵也不思天下莫强於
信義不惇信義而以力之强弱分成敗可乎苞
===
桑之繫略而不圖蠶食之虞怵而未已三國之
務亦末矣卒之鄧為之滅蔡為之虜鄭為之服
役其皆自貽伊戚者乎吾于周公得膺懲之訓
焉于宣王見采芑之師焉禦外以安內蓄威以
昭德先王之經世也有遺烈矣寧有惴惴焉徒
懼如兹會也聖人于此有深慨焉特書於冊以
示經斯世者可以觀夷夏盛衰之機也可以明
强本治內柔服遠人之道也不然外相會不志
此獨奚為志之哉抑周之盛時楚居南服未梗
punctuated: 也。而其可恃以無恐者，不有自治之道乎？使能任賢明政，而樹德以奠邦；輯眾善鄰，而協謀以禦侮，則人和固於城郭，忠信堅於甲胄。荆楚雖大，何懼焉？而乃好會徒煩，訂謨罔協，不虞弗戒，空懷剥牀之憂。豈以楚地五千里，其大不可敵也？不思天下莫大於理，不循天理而以地之大小分勝負，可乎？先事弗備，徒懾門庭之寇，抑以帶甲數十萬，其强不可敵也？不思天下莫强於信義，不惇信義而以力之强弱分成敗，可乎？苞桑之繫，略而不圖；蠶食之虞，怵而未已。三國之務亦末矣！卒之，鄧為之滅，蔡為之虜，鄭為之服役，其皆自貽伊戚者乎？吾于周公得膺懲之訓焉，于宣王見《采芑》之師焉。禦外以安內，蓄威以昭德，先王之經世也有遺烈矣。寧有惴惴焉徒懼如兹會也？聖人于此有深慨焉，特書於冊，以示經斯世者，可以觀夷夏盛衰之機也，可以明强本治內、柔服遠人之道也。不然，外相會不志，此獨奚為志之哉？抑周之盛時，楚居南服，未梗
translation_en:
…it is its power. Yet did they not possess a way of governing themselves well upon which they could rely to be free from fear? Had they employed worthy men and made their government enlightened, establishing virtue to secure their states; had they united their people and maintained good relations with their neighbors, coordinating plans to repel aggression, then harmony among their people would have been stronger than city walls, and loyalty and trustworthiness firmer than armor and helmets. Though Jing-Chu was great, what would there have been to fear? Instead, their meetings of amity brought only trouble, and the plans they agreed upon produced no concerted action. They took no precautions against the unexpected, merely fretting over danger that would strip away their very foundations, like a bed being stripped away. Was it because Chu possessed territory extending five thousand li that they thought its greatness impossible to withstand? They failed to consider that nothing under Heaven is greater than principle. Could they disregard Heaven’s principle and judge victory or defeat by the size of a state’s territory? Making no preparations beforehand, they merely trembled at the enemy at their gates. Or was it because Chu had several hundred thousand armored soldiers that they thought its strength impossible to withstand? They failed to consider that nothing under Heaven is stronger than trustworthiness and righteousness. Could they neglect to cultivate these and judge success or failure by relative military strength?

They neglected to plan how to secure themselves, as though bound fast to a clump of mulberry trees, yet never ceased trembling at the prospect of being eaten away like leaves by silkworms. The three states concerned themselves with mere incidentals! In the end, Deng was destroyed by Chu, Cai was taken captive, and Zheng was subjected to its service. Had they not all brought this misery upon themselves? In the Duke of Zhou I find the teaching of striking and chastising aggressors; in King Xuan I see the army celebrated in “Gathering Millet” (Cai qi). Repelling external threats to secure the interior, and cultivating military might to manifest virtue—the former kings left enduring achievements in their ordering of the world. How could they have merely trembled in fear, as those at this meeting did?

The Sage felt profound sorrow over this and specially recorded it in the annals to instruct those who would bring order to the world. Here one may observe the pivotal workings of the rise and decline of the Yi peoples and the Xia states; here one may understand the way to strengthen the foundations, order internal affairs, and win the allegiance of distant peoples through benevolent treatment. Otherwise, since meetings among other states are not recorded, why was this one alone recorded? Moreover, when Zhou flourished, Chu occupied the southern domain and had not yet become defiant…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
也及其衰也楚氛惡矣玆鄧之會寔以肇中國
陵夷之端向非九合一匡之功諸夏之厄殆不
止虜蔡滅鄧已也然則流禍中國也其三國乎
而中國之幸不爲楚者桓之賜也故曰微管仲
吾其被髮左衽矣嗚呼此春秋所以作乎
滕子來朝桓公二年齊人來歸鄆讙龜陰
田定公十年
許尚靜
同考試官教諭張批垂法示公咸聖人不得
===
已焉蓋一經大旨攸繫言之明潔而無費辭是之
取爾
考試官教諭黃批得謹嚴體
考試官學正林批文約而盡
聖人脩經有所以垂大法者有所以示大公者
觀滕侯朝魯而稱子齊人歸邑而書來聖人垂
法示公之意何如哉慨昔鍾巫之變桓公實與
焉滕也不能致辟於魯顧光鄰國而來朝惟是
與賊爲黨有不容於或貸者然命德討罪權出
punctuated:
也。及其衰也，楚氛惡矣。玆鄧之會，寔以肇中國陵夷之端。向非九合一匡之功，諸夏之厄殆不止虜蔡滅鄧已也。然則流禍中國也，其三國乎？而中國之幸不爲楚者，桓之賜也。故曰：「微管仲，吾其被髮左衽矣。」嗚呼！此春秋所以作乎？
滕子來朝，桓公二年。齊人來歸鄆讙龜陰田，定公十年。
許尚靜
同考試官教諭張批：垂法示公，咸聖人不得已焉。蓋一經大旨攸繫，言之明潔而無費辭，是之取爾。
考試官教諭黃批：得謹嚴體。
考試官學正林批：文約而盡。
聖人脩經，有所以垂大法者，有所以示大公者。觀滕侯朝魯而稱子，齊人歸邑而書來，聖人垂法示公之意何如哉？慨昔鍾巫之變，桓公實與焉。滕也不能致辟於魯，顧光鄰國而來朝。惟是與賊爲黨，有不容於或貸者。然命德討罪，權出
translation_en:
…Yet when Zhou declined, the baleful influence of Chu became severe. This meeting at Deng indeed initiated the decline of the Central States. Had it not been for the achievement of assembling the lords nine times and bringing order to all under Heaven, the calamities of the Xia states would probably not have stopped at the capture of the ruler of Cai and the destruction of Deng. Was it not these three states, then, that spread disaster through the Central States? That the Central States were fortunate enough not to fall under Chu was Duke Huan’s benefaction. Thus it is said: “Were it not for Guan Zhong, we would wear our hair loose and fasten our robes on the left.” Alas! Was this why the Spring and Autumn Annals was composed?

“The Viscount of Teng came to pay court.” Second year of Duke Huan. “Men of Qi came to return the lands of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin.” Tenth year of Duke Ding.

Xu Shangjing

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “Bequeathing standards and displaying impartiality were both things the Sage had no choice but to do. Herein lies the central purport of the entire classic. The discussion is clear and concise, without wasted words; this is why I select it.”

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: “It achieves a careful and rigorous style.”

Comment by Examiner Lin, School Director: “The writing is concise yet exhaustive.”

In revising the classic, the Sage had ways of bequeathing great standards and ways of displaying supreme impartiality. Consider how the Marquis of Teng paid court to Lu but was designated ‘Viscount,’ and how the men of Qi returned settlements and the text recorded that they ‘came.’ What intentions did the Sage have in thus bequeathing standards and displaying impartiality? Alas, Duke Huan was indeed implicated in the former incident at Zhongwu. Teng could not bring punishment upon Lu, but instead came to pay court, lending lustre to the neighbouring state. In thus joining the criminal’s faction, he committed an offence that could admit of no pardon. Yet the authority to confer honours upon the virtuous and punish the guilty emanates …

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
於上可也聖人春秋之匹夫耳降侯而子寧不
幾於僭乎殊不知春秋天子之事也假史脩經
王法攸寓是故於諸侯之滅理廢倫者不奉天
恭罰以黜其爵焉則何以垂大法於後世哉噫
僭之初生也由於分之不定夫子黜滕侯而比
諸夷狄此名實所由以定與黃帝之伐蚩尤大
禹之戮防風事殊而理一也何僭之有至若夾
谷之會孔子寔相之齊也不敢有加於魯遂歸
侵疆以謝過惟是順理化强有不容於或揜者
===
然表功嘉績事公於人可矣春秋夫子之筆削
也特書曰來寧不避夫嫌乎殊不知聖人以天
自處也視人猶已大同無間是故於諸侯之感
化効順者不卽事據實而書于册焉則何以示
大公於天下哉噫人之避嫌也由於內之不足
夫子書來歸以志其心服此盛德所由以著與
書紀大舜之格苗傳稱文王之降崇功同而體
一也何嫌之有是則黜人之爵而弗為專序已
之績而無所避此春秋所由作夫子所以為聖
punctuated: 於上可也。聖人，春秋之匹夫耳，降侯而子，寧不幾於僭乎？殊不知《春秋》，天子之事也。假史脩經，王法攸寓。是故於諸侯之滅理廢倫者，不奉天恭罰以黜其爵焉，則何以垂大法於後世哉？噫！僭之初生也，由於分之不定。夫子黜滕侯而比諸夷狄，此名實所由以定，與黃帝之伐蚩尤、大禹之戮防風，事殊而理一也，何僭之有？至若夾谷之會，孔子寔相之，齊也不敢有加於魯，遂歸侵疆以謝過。惟是順理化强，有不容於或揜者。然表功嘉績，事公於人可矣。《春秋》，夫子之筆削也，特書曰「來」，寧不避夫嫌乎？殊不知聖人以天自處也，視人猶已，大同無間。是故於諸侯之感化効順者，不卽事據實而書于册焉，則何以示大公於天下哉？噫！人之避嫌也，由於內之不足。夫子書「來歸」以志其心服，此盛德所由以著，與《書》紀大舜之格苗、傳稱文王之降崇，功同而體一也，何嫌之有？是則黜人之爵而弗為專，序已之績而無所避，此《春秋》所由作，夫子所以為聖
translation_en:
…it is permissible when authority rests with the sovereign. Yet the Sage was merely a commoner in the Spring and Autumn period: in reducing a marquis to the rank of viscount, did he not verge on usurpation? This objection fails to recognize that the Spring and Autumn Annals concerns the business of the Son of Heaven. Drawing upon historical records to compile the Classic, he embodied therein the laws of kingship. Thus, when feudal lords destroyed moral principle and abandoned proper human relationships, unless he reverently carried out Heaven’s punishment by degrading their ranks, how could he transmit the great law to later generations? Alas! Usurpation first arises because distinctions of status are not settled. The Master degraded the Marquis of Teng and placed him on a level with the peoples beyond the civilized realm; thereby titles and realities were brought into accord. Compared with the Yellow Emperor’s campaign against Chiyou and Yu the Great’s execution of Fangfeng, the events differed, but the principle was one. What usurpation was there?

As for the meeting at Jiagu, Confucius indeed assisted in its ceremonies. Qi dared not impose upon Lu and consequently returned the territory it had seized, to acknowledge its wrongdoing. Such conformity to principle and transformation of the strong cannot be left obscured. Yet, in commending achievements and praising accomplishments, it is fitting to leave the matter to the impartial judgment of others. The Spring and Autumn Annals was edited by the Master himself: in expressly writing “came,” should he not have avoided the suspicion of self-praise? This objection fails to recognize that the Sage takes Heaven as his own standpoint. He regards others as himself, in complete unity without division. Thus, when feudal lords responded to his transforming influence and rendered obedience, unless he recorded the events in accordance with the facts, how could he demonstrate supreme impartiality to all under Heaven? Alas! People avoid suspicion because of an insufficiency within themselves. The Master wrote “came to return” to record their heartfelt submission; thereby his abundant virtue was made manifest. This was like the account in the Book of Documents of the great Shun bringing the Miao to submission, and the tradition’s praise of King Wen’s subjugation of Chong: the achievement was the same and its essential character was one. What grounds for suspicion were there? Thus he degraded another’s rank without acting arbitrarily, and recounted his own achievements without anything to avoid. This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals was composed, and why the Master was a sage…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
也歟抑考之夫子嘗曰知我罪我者其惟春秋
乎又曰知我者其惟天乎夫惟求知于天則齊
物我通古今所往皆安而何異同之可議夫惟
付其知罪於人則筆削予奪見諸行事深切著
明復何擅黜之可疑顧惟定公不能舉國以聽
俾聖神功化僅見於章章之歸田豈不重可慨
夫
禮記
是以君子恭敬撙節退讓以明禮
王賛襄
考試官敎諭黃批講恭敬撙節退讓處詞
不費而意足可取
考試官學正林批以為克已復禮之學良
是惟得此旨乃有此作
觀君子篤治躬之道而禮之義昭矣夫禮無本
不立也君子反躬以自治則禮之情得矣其義
不由是而著明乎記者之意謂夫惟天下無非
禮之事故君子致凝禮之功亦不過反求諸其
punctuated:
也歟？抑考之，夫子嘗曰：「知我罪我者，其惟春秋乎！」又曰：「知我者，其惟天乎！」夫惟求知于天，則齊物我，通古今，所往皆安，而何異同之可議？夫惟付其知罪於人，則筆削予奪，見諸行事，深切著明，復何擅黜之可疑？顧惟定公不能舉國以聽，俾聖神功化僅見於章章之歸田，豈不重可慨夫！
禮記
是以君子恭敬撙節退讓以明禮。
王賛襄
考試官敎諭黃批：講恭敬撙節退讓處，詞不費而意足，可取。
考試官學正林批：以為克已復禮之學，良是。惟得此旨，乃有此作。
觀君子篤治躬之道，而禮之義昭矣。夫禮無本不立也，君子反躬以自治，則禮之情得矣，其義不由是而著明乎？記者之意謂，夫惟天下無非禮之事，故君子致凝禮之功，亦不過反求諸其
translation_en:
…is this what makes him a sage? Moreover, on examining the matter, the Master once said: “Those who understand me and those who condemn me—will it not be through the Spring and Autumn Annals?” He also said: “Is it not Heaven alone that understands me?” Precisely because he sought understanding from Heaven, he placed others and himself on equal terms, comprehended past and present, and was at ease wherever he went. What grounds, then, could there be for disputing his differing treatments? Precisely because he left understanding or condemning him to others, his inclusion and deletion, his bestowal and withholding of recognition, were embodied in his treatment of events, profound, incisive, and manifest. What grounds remained for suspecting him of arbitrarily stripping rulers of their ranks? Yet Duke Ding could not bring the entire state to heed him, so that the sage’s wondrous achievements and transforming influence were manifest only in the conspicuous return of the fields. Is this not deeply lamentable!
Record of Rites
“Thus the gentleman makes ritual propriety clear through reverence, respect, restraint, moderation, deference, and yielding.”
Wang Zanxiang
Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: “In explaining reverence, respect, restraint, moderation, deference, and yielding, the wording is economical while the meaning is fully conveyed. This is commendable.”
Comment by Examiner Lin, School Instructor: “To regard this as the learning of overcoming oneself and returning to ritual propriety is indeed correct. Only by grasping this purport could one produce such an essay.”
When we observe how earnestly the gentleman pursues the way of cultivating himself, the meaning of ritual propriety becomes clear. Ritual propriety cannot stand without a foundation. When the gentleman turns inward to discipline himself, he grasps its true substance. Does its meaning not thereby become manifest? The compiler’s intention is to say that, since nothing in the world lies outside the affairs of ritual propriety, the gentleman’s work of bringing ritual propriety to fulfillment amounts simply to seeking it within his own…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
身耳是故由齋莊有恭之名君子與人有禮而
不侮執事有恪而不懈肅肅乎盡其恭而恭焉
由主一有敬之名君子明裡以直其内慎獨以
防其外洞洞乎盡其敬而敬焉知欲不可從也
則損之又損而節以制度不役志於多儀蓋有
克而去之也何撙節如之知志不可滿也則雖
休勿休而卑以自牧不徑情於所接蓋有推而
遠之也何退讓如之君子於此其治躬之道可
謂盡矣而謂之明禮何哉蓋禮反其始所以著
===
誠去偽者此也惟恭與敬則中正無邪而一德
之聚有所以立其本者禮主其減所以領惡全
好者此也惟撙節退讓則敬恭無失而凡衆之
動有所以慎其出者故不必俎豆之是事也而
大禮必簡與天地同節者本諸身而可見不必
周旋以為容也而至禮不爭與秋冬同義者即
其事而可知禮不於是而有明乎是則禮之於
人其用為甚博而君子之庸禮也其道為甚約
信乎禮切於人而不可以外有所求也抑禮者
punctuated: 身耳。是故由齋莊有恭之名，君子與人有禮而不侮，執事有恪而不懈，肅肅乎盡其恭而恭焉。由主一有敬之名，君子明裡以直其内，慎獨以防其外，洞洞乎盡其敬而敬焉。知欲不可從也，則損之又損，而節以制度，不役志於多儀，蓋有克而去之也，何撙節如之！知志不可滿也，則雖休勿休，而卑以自牧，不徑情於所接，蓋有推而遠之也，何退讓如之！君子於此，其治躬之道可謂盡矣，而謂之明禮，何哉？蓋禮反其始，所以著誠去偽者此也。惟恭與敬，則中正無邪，而一德之聚有所以立其本者。禮主其減，所以領惡全好者此也。惟撙節退讓，則敬恭無失，而凡衆之動有所以慎其出者。故不必俎豆之是事也，而大禮必簡，與天地同節者，本諸身而可見；不必周旋以為容也，而至禮不爭，與秋冬同義者，即其事而可知。禮不於是而有明乎？是則禮之於人，其用為甚博，而君子之庸禮也，其道為甚約。信乎禮切於人，而不可以外有所求也！抑禮者，
translation_en:
…his own person alone. Thus, from solemn composure comes what is called respectful deportment. The gentleman treats others with ritual propriety and does not insult them; he attends to affairs conscientiously and without slackness. Solemnly, he exercises his respect to the utmost and remains respectful. From concentrating on the One comes what is called reverence. The gentleman clarifies principle [?] to make his inner self upright, and is watchful over himself when alone to guard his outward conduct. With earnest attentiveness, he exercises his reverence to the utmost and remains reverent. Knowing that desires must not be indulged, he diminishes them again and again and restrains them through established rules, without enslaving his will to a multiplicity of ceremonies. He thus masters and removes them: what restraint could equal this! Knowing that his aspirations must not become overweening, he does not rest content even when praised, but nurtures himself through humility and does not act on unchecked feelings in his dealings with others. He thus pushes such tendencies away and keeps them at a distance: what yielding and deference could equal this!

In these respects, the gentleman’s way of governing himself may be called complete. But why is this termed making ritual propriety clear? Ritual returns to its beginnings: this is how it manifests sincerity and removes pretense. Through respect and reverence alone, one becomes centered and upright, free from perversity; the gathering of these qualities into a single virtue provides the means to establish ritual’s foundation. Ritual takes reduction as its guiding principle: this is how it checks what is bad [?] and preserves what is good intact. Through restraint, yielding, and deference alone, reverence and respect remain faultless, and there is a means to exercise care in the expression of all one’s manifold activities.

Thus, one need not concern oneself solely with sacrificial stands and vessels: the greatest ritual is necessarily simple, sharing the measured order of Heaven and Earth, and this can be seen when it is rooted in one’s own person. Nor need one make movements and turns into a display of deportment: consummate ritual is free from contention, sharing the significance of autumn and winter, and this can be understood through one’s actual conduct. Is ritual propriety not thereby made clear? Thus, although ritual has exceedingly broad applications in human life, the gentleman’s way of practicing it is exceedingly concise. Truly, ritual bears intimately upon the person, and one cannot seek it outside oneself! Moreover, ritual is…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
節文而已恭敬撙節而節生焉退讓而文生焉
然必能敬而後能節必能節而後能讓敬讓立
而禮行焉故此亦足以觀禮矣然究而言之則
克己復禮之學莫近於是君子何可以不盡心
乎爾
六者非性也感於物而后動是故先王慎
所以感之者故禮以道其志樂以和其
聲政以一其行刑以防其姦禮樂刑政
其極一也所以同民心而出治道也
===
海瑞
考試官教諭黃批此題不難鋪敘成篇但
覺冗長可厭理明辭暢無踰此作
考試官學正林批講慎感處不露而意象
自見且以閑養分配亦是正理錄之
記者原先王謹於治人之情而著其法之盡善
也夫人心易動而物之感多變也先王慎其事
則思善其治而法焉有不善者哉記樂記者之
意蓋謂人性本善而物至無方及夫喜怒哀樂
punctuated:
節文而已。恭敬撙節，而節生焉；退讓，而文生焉。然必能敬而後能節，必能節而後能讓。敬讓立而禮行焉，故此亦足以觀禮矣。然究而言之，則克己復禮之學莫近於是，君子何可以不盡心乎爾？

六者非性也，感於物而后動。是故先王慎所以感之者，故禮以道其志，樂以和其聲，政以一其行，刑以防其姦。禮樂刑政，其極一也，所以同民心而出治道也。

海瑞

考試官教諭黃批：「此題不難鋪敘成篇，但覺冗長可厭。理明辭暢，無踰此作。」

考試官學正林批：「講慎感處不露，而意象自見，且以閑養分配，亦是正理，錄之。」

記者原先王謹於治人之情，而著其法之盡善也。夫人心易動，而物之感多變也。先王慎其事，則思善其治，而法焉有不善者哉？記樂記者之意，蓋謂人性本善，而物至無方，及夫喜怒哀樂
translation_en:
…is simply regulation and patterned expression. Reverence and restraint give rise to regulation; deference gives rise to patterned expression. Yet one must be capable of reverence before one can exercise restraint, and capable of restraint before one can show deference. When reverence and deference are established, ritual is practiced. Thus these, too, suffice to reveal ritual. Ultimately, nothing comes closer than this to the learning of overcoming the self and returning to ritual. How could a gentleman fail to devote his whole heart to it?

“These six are not human nature itself; they become active only when stirred by external things. Therefore the former kings took care over what stirred people. Thus ritual guides their aspirations, music harmonizes their voices, government unifies their conduct, and punishments prevent their wrongdoing. Ritual, music, punishments, and government have one ultimate end: to unite the people’s hearts and bring forth the way of good government.”

Hai Rui 海瑞

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor of a Confucian School at the county level: “It is not difficult to elaborate this topic into a complete essay, but the result readily seems tedious and tiresomely long. For clarity of reasoning and fluency of expression, no essay surpasses this one.”

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor of a Confucian School at the subprefectural level: “Its discussion of taking care over what stirs people is unobtrusive, yet its meaning and conception emerge of themselves. Moreover, its allocation of the discussion between restraint and nurture accords with correct principle. Selected for inclusion.”

The author of the Record examines why the former kings were careful in governing human emotions and makes manifest the consummate goodness of their methods. People’s hearts are easily moved, and the influences of external things vary greatly. Since the former kings took care over this matter, they sought to perfect their governance. How, then, could their methods have been anything but good? The intention of the author who composed the Record of Music was, it would seem, to say that human nature is originally good, while external things come upon it in unpredictable ways; and when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
愛敬之既發則非人生而靜天命之本然蓋其
應感起物而動有不能以自已者其機如此而
先王何以治之哉惟人心之危則養之不可以
不周惟物化之易則閑之不可以不至于于是有
禮焉習之於其靜而志以之道無弗節者有樂
焉效之於其動而聲以之和無或乖焉蓋養之
如此其周也懼其行之弗協也齊以政以一之
而使之日遷乎善懼其姦之弗率也明五刑以
防之而使之日遠乎罪蓋閑之如此其至也先
===
王之於民也由其有六情之感是以有四事之
施斯蓋異情而同功其爲慎感之道一也夫然
後政以德孚觀其所感而丕應傒志矣何民而
不同乎此心哉道以政通極其所至而四達不
悖矣何治而不出于此道哉蓋至是而禮樂可
作刑可措而化可昭焉況其在聲音之間者乎
抑考禮運敘聖人脩德治情之政蓋譬之於田
耕種耨穫猶以爲未也必食而肥焉斯已矣然
後協于天下謂之大順則夫人情所係豈不誠
punctuated:
愛敬之既發，則非人生而靜、天命之本然。蓋其應感起物而動，有不能以自已者，其機如此，而先王何以治之哉？惟人心之危，則養之不可以不周；惟物化之易，則閑之不可以不至。于于是有禮焉，習之於其靜，而志以之道，無弗節者；有樂焉，效之於其動，而聲以之和，無或乖焉。蓋養之如此其周也。懼其行之弗協也，齊以政以一之，而使之日遷乎善；懼其姦之弗率也，明五刑以防之，而使之日遠乎罪。蓋閑之如此其至也。先王之於民也，由其有六情之感，是以有四事之施。斯蓋異情而同功，其爲慎感之道一也。夫然後政以德孚，觀其所感，而丕應傒志矣，何民而不同乎此心哉？道以政通，極其所至，而四達不悖矣，何治而不出于此道哉？蓋至是而禮樂可作，刑可措，而化可昭焉，況其在聲音之間者乎？
抑考《禮運》敘聖人脩德治情之政，蓋譬之於田，耕種耨穫，猶以爲未也，必食而肥焉，斯已矣。然後協于天下，謂之大順。則夫人情所係，豈不誠
translation_en:
…once love and reverence have arisen, this is no longer the original condition endowed by Heaven, in which human beings are still at birth. Responding to stimuli, people are stirred by external things and cannot restrain themselves. Such being the workings of their feelings, how did the former kings govern them? Precisely because the human heart is precarious, its cultivation must be comprehensive; precisely because external things can so readily transform it, its safeguarding must be thorough. Thus [?] there were rites: practiced in stillness, they guided the will, leaving nothing unregulated. There was music: brought into effect in movement, it harmonized the sounds, leaving nothing discordant. So comprehensive was their cultivation. Fearing that people's conduct would not accord with what was right, they ordered and unified them through government, causing them daily to advance toward goodness. Fearing that their wickedness would keep them from obedience, they made the Five Punishments clear as a preventive measure, causing them daily to distance themselves from crime. So thorough was their safeguarding.
In dealing with the people, the former kings employed these four measures because people were susceptible to the stirring of the six emotions. These measures differed in character but shared a common achievement: they were one in their way of attending carefully to what stirs people's feelings. Only then did government win trust through virtue: observing what moved the people, it elicited a great response and fulfilled their aspirations [?]. What people would not share this heart? The Way was made effective through government; reaching its fullest extent, it extended in all four directions without contradiction. What good governance would not proceed from this Way? At this point, rites and music could flourish, punishments could be laid aside, and moral transformation could become manifest. How much more would this be true of what finds expression in sounds!
Moreover, examining the account in the Evolution of Rites (Liyun) of the sages' government through cultivating virtue and regulating feelings, we find that it compares this to working a field. Plowing, sowing, weeding, and harvesting were still considered insufficient: only when people had eaten and grown well nourished was the work complete. Only then was harmony attained throughout the realm, called the Great Concord. Surely, then, what is bound up with human feelings is truly…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
重矣哉夫治民不求諸其本而曰吾有以治之
舍術數則刑名而已是烏能得其化服哉
第貳場
論
聖人人倫之至
胡庭蘭
同考試官教諭江批是題人皆知之但命意
不得要領語多虚蔓此以道不遠人為主渾確詞
旨俱自胸中流出且一至字發揮明盡蓋深得孟
===
氏之意是非體認特精見理獨到者不能也録傳
考試官教諭黃批純正粹雅自是大家氣
象
考試官學正林批論有學識非漫然隨衆
者
道極於聖人也而聖人不遠人以為道於是立
人極於天下夫聖人亦人也而道曷為極之也
以其盡人也盡人者不遠乎人也不遠人而人
盡斯人之至也人之至者人之極也聖人立人
punctuated:
重矣哉！夫治民不求諸其本，而曰吾有以治之，舍術數則刑名而已，是烏能得其化服哉？

第貳場
論
聖人人倫之至
胡庭蘭

同考試官教諭江批：是題人皆知之，但命意不得要領，語多虚蔓。此以道不遠人為主，渾確，詞旨俱自胸中流出，且一至字發揮明盡，蓋深得孟氏之意。是非體認特精、見理獨到者不能也。録傳。

考試官教諭黃批：純正粹雅，自是大家氣象。

考試官學正林批：論有學識，非漫然隨衆者。

道極於聖人也，而聖人不遠人以為道，於是立人極於天下。夫聖人亦人也，而道曷為極之也？以其盡人也。盡人者不遠乎人也，不遠人而人盡，斯人之至也。人之至者，人之極也。聖人立人
translation_en:
…weighty indeed! If one governs the people without seeking the root of government, yet says, “I have the means to govern them,” those means can only be manipulative techniques or punishments and the enforcement of official duties. How could these bring the people to submit through moral transformation?

Second Session
Discourse
“The Sage Is the Culmination of Human Relationships”
Hu Tinglan

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Instructor: Everyone understands this topic, but their conceptions fail to grasp its essentials, and their language is often empty and diffuse. This essay takes “the Way does not depart from humanity” as its central idea and is both integrated and precise. Its wording and meaning flow entirely from the writer’s own mind. Moreover, it expounds the single word “culmination” clearly and exhaustively, profoundly grasping Mengzi’s meaning. Such writing is possible only for someone whose personal apprehension is exceptionally refined and whose insight into principle is distinctive. Record it for circulation.

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: Pure and correct, refined and elegant: it has the unmistakable bearing of a master.

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: This discourse displays learning and discernment; it is not the work of someone who heedlessly follows the crowd.

The Way reaches its culmination in the sage, yet the sage does not depart from humanity in practicing the Way. Thus he establishes the ultimate human standard throughout the world. The sage, too, is a human being: why, then, does the Way reach its culmination in him? Because he fully realizes what it means to be human. One who fully realizes humanity does not depart from human beings. To remain close to humanity and fully realize it is the culmination of being human. This culmination is the ultimate human standard. The sage establishes the human…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
極夫豈不欲人人之為聖人而人之求聖人者
於人之外是以道遠乎人而聖人益不可幾及
而聖人立極之意孤孟子憂之故曰聖人人倫
之至夫曰人倫則知遠人非道求之人倫所以
求聖也曰至則知惟聖盡倫未至乎聖不可言
倫也今夫言天者物之父生物之至也言地者
物之母成物之至也言聖人者人之命盡人之
至也夫天則高矣而曰父地則廣矣而曰母天
地之至也且不能外於物聖人獨能外人以盡
===
人耶何人之自小其身也則望聖人者甚大自
忽其倫也則視聖人者太深故二三子以孔子
為有隱而公孫丑謂道若登天甚矣知之難也
雖堯舜之民比屋可封然但使之由而已未能
使知也夫堯舜不能使人之知孔孟不能釋有
隱之疑登天之惑無惑乎聖道之不明也道不
明而後處士橫議邪說浸淫學術之壞可勝言
哉慕高遠者則虛談性命曰至也不知性命卽
人倫之蘊使道之高遠而外人倫是異端也非
punctuated: 極，夫豈不欲人人之為聖人？而人之求聖人者，於人之外，是以道遠乎人，而聖人益不可幾及，而聖人立極之意孤。孟子憂之，故曰：「聖人，人倫之至。」夫曰人倫，則知遠人非道，求之人倫，所以求聖也；曰至，則知惟聖盡倫，未至乎聖，不可言倫也。今夫言天者，物之父，生物之至也；言地者，物之母，成物之至也；言聖人者，人之命，盡人之至也。夫天則高矣，而曰父；地則廣矣，而曰母。天地之至也，且不能外於物，聖人獨能外人以盡人耶？何人之自小其身也，則望聖人者甚大；自忽其倫也，則視聖人者太深。故二三子以孔子為有隱，而公孫丑謂道若登天。甚矣，知之難也！雖堯舜之民比屋可封，然但使之由而已，未能使知也。夫堯舜不能使人之知，孔孟不能釋有隱之疑、登天之惑，無惑乎聖道之不明也。道不明，而後處士橫議，邪說浸淫，學術之壞可勝言哉！慕高遠者，則虛談性命，曰至也，不知性命卽人倫之蘊。使道之高遠而外人倫，是異端也，非
translation_en:
…the ultimate standard: surely his intention was that everyone should become a sage? Yet those who seek to become sages seek beyond the human realm. Thus the Way grows distant from humanity, sages become ever less possible to approach, and the sage’s intention in establishing the ultimate standard is left unfulfilled. Mengzi was troubled by this, and therefore said: “The sage is the perfection of human relationships.” The words “human relationships” tell us that what departs from humanity is not the Way: seeking within human relationships is how one seeks sagehood. The word “perfection” tells us that only a sage fully realizes these relationships; before attaining sagehood, one cannot claim to have fulfilled them.

Now, when we speak of Heaven, it is the father of all things, the perfection of bringing things to life; when we speak of Earth, it is the mother of all things, the perfection of bringing things to completion; when we speak of the sage, he is the life of humanity, the perfection of fully realizing what it is to be human. Heaven is lofty, yet we call it father; Earth is vast, yet we call it mother. Even Heaven and Earth, in their perfection, cannot stand outside the things they produce. Could the sage alone stand outside humanity in order to realize humanity fully? Why is it that people belittle themselves and therefore regard sages as exceedingly great, or neglect their own relationships and therefore regard sages as excessively profound? Thus Confucius’s disciples thought that he was concealing something from them, and Gongsun Chou said that the Way was like ascending to Heaven. How very difficult it is to understand!

Although the people under Yao and Shun were such that every household could have been granted a fief, they were merely enabled to follow the Way; they could not be made to understand it. Since Yao and Shun could not make people understand, and Confucius and Mengzi could not dispel the suspicion that something was being concealed or the misconception that the Way was like ascending to Heaven, it is no wonder that the Way of the sages remains obscure. Once the Way became obscure, scholars out of office advanced unrestrained arguments, and pernicious doctrines gradually spread. Could the corruption of learning be adequately described? Those who admire the lofty and remote engage in empty talk of human nature and destiny, calling this perfection. They do not understand that human nature and destiny are precisely what lies within human relationships. If the Way, in its loftiness and remoteness, lies outside human relationships, this is heterodox teaching, not…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
明不自用
疇咨海內
懍初服之投艱
延攬日中宜
大人之繼照為德不忘其舊用人必盡其長
念
先帝之所遺
起愚臣於旣老桑榆且迫恐孤
四世之恩犬馬何能尚銜一飯之報事必盡
===
乎方寸言不妄於生平抱此區區何能已
已以茲末議遂復
上陳伏願
皇覽丕昭見葵心之有在
帝謨克廣采葑體以無遺萬有一其必行非臣
獨荷十得五而猶慰為
國有人臣光無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屏營之至謹具疏隨
punctuated: 明不自用，疇咨海內。懍初服之投艱，延攬日中，宜大人之繼照。為德不忘其舊，用人必盡其長。念先帝之所遺，起愚臣於旣老。桑榆且迫，恐孤四世之恩；犬馬何能，尚銜一飯之報。事必盡乎方寸，言不妄於生平。抱此區區，何能已已？以茲末議，遂復上陳。伏願皇覽丕昭，見葵心之有在；帝謨克廣，采葑體以無遺。萬有一其必行，非臣獨荷；十得五而猶慰，為國有人。臣光無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹具疏隨
translation_en:
…enlightened, yet not relying solely on your own judgment, you consult widely throughout the realm. Mindful of the difficulties entrusted to you upon first assuming the throne, you recruit worthy men as the sun reaches its zenith, fittingly continuing the illumination of a great ruler. In practicing virtue, you do not forget old associates; in employing men, you make full use of their strengths. Remembering those left by the late emperor, you recalled your foolish servant after he had already grown old. As the twilight of life approaches, I fear failing to repay the grace of four imperial reigns. What can one as lowly as a dog or horse accomplish? Yet I still cherish the obligation to repay even a single meal. In every undertaking I must exhaust my heartfelt devotion; throughout my life I have spoken without falsehood. Holding this modest sincerity within me, how could I desist [?]?

With these humble proposals, I therefore once more submit my views to the throne. I humbly pray that your imperial scrutiny may shine brightly and discern my devotion, like the sunflower turning toward the sun; that your imperial counsels may grow broad, accepting what is useful without rejecting it for its defects, as one gathers turnip greens despite their roots. If even one proposal in ten thousand is put into practice, your servant alone will not be the beneficiary. If five out of ten prove acceptable, I shall still be comforted that the state has men to serve it. Your servant Guang, gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your Majesty, cannot contain his fervent emotion and trembling awe. I respectfully prepare this submission to accompany…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
表上
進以
聞
第參塲
策
第一問
王賛襄
考試官敎諭黃批
大明會典自是會聚
===
國朝諸典并諸條例爲書以便遵覽與周禮體裁本自不同子言
具有折衷末意尤見忠愛錄之不獨以其文也
考試官學正林批策涉
制書事關
本朝士子類於沿習帖括得之故多縱筆成篇而無復考定規裁
之意此篇據經討古不昧時宜俊傑之士也
繼天而作其體大繼聖而述其法詳大其
體故道可得而冒也化可得而裁也物可
得而昭也極可得而建也詳其法故類可
punctuated:
表上進，以聞。
第參塲，策，第一問。王賛襄。
考試官敎諭黃批：大明會典自是會聚國朝諸典并諸條例爲書，以便遵覽，與周禮體裁本自不同。子言具有折衷，末意尤見忠愛。錄之，不獨以其文也。
考試官學正林批：策涉制書，事關本朝，士子類於沿習帖括得之，故多縱筆成篇，而無復考定規裁之意。此篇據經討古，不昧時宜，俊傑之士也。
繼天而作，其體大；繼聖而述，其法詳。大其體，故道可得而冒也，化可得而裁也，物可得而昭也，極可得而建也；詳其法，故類可
translation_en:
…submitted with the memorial for Your Majesty’s hearing.
Third Session: Policy Essay, First Question. Wang Zanxiang.
Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor (jiaoyu): The Collected Statutes of the Great Ming brings together the statutes and regulations of our dynasty into a book for convenient consultation and observance. Its form is fundamentally different from that of the Rites of Zhou. Your discussion shows balanced judgment throughout, and its closing sentiments particularly reveal your loyalty and devotion. It is not solely for its literary qualities that this essay has been selected.
Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor (xuezheng): This policy question concerns imperial enactments and matters of our own dynasty. Candidates generally derive their knowledge from habitual study of examination compositions; hence many write freely until they have produced an essay, without further thought of examining the facts or determining the proper framework. This essay draws upon the Classics and investigates antiquity without losing sight of what is appropriate to the times. Its author is a man of outstanding talent.
To carry on Heaven’s work and institute something new requires a grand framework; to carry forward the sages’ work and transmit it requires detailed methods. With a grand framework, the Way can encompass all, transforming influences can be properly shaped, things can be made manifest, and the supreme standard can be established. With detailed methods, categories can…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
得而舉也政可得而齊也禮可得而因也
道可得而乂也故惟聖而後經天下之體
立惟明而後守天下之法融記曰作者之
謂聖述者之謂明明聖者述作之謂也請
得以是復明問焉蓋自昔人君定命於艱
難之際勞心於草昧之初事熟於見聞之
下慮深於憂患之餘其於保大定功以為
燕翼計者蓋莫不有典章焉顧其立國之
初萬務叢舉事每病於不給承平則愈復
===
闊略物忘其舊率多簡陋之風故以西漢
之盛二百年無服章之制雖唐六典亦蒙
宇文之舊徒文具而無所設施宋會要不
定朝會之儀至熙寧而始議其禮其他固
不足徵也於惟
皇祖躬
上聖之資雄曠古之績盡倫盡制有綱有紀故
其見於制作也有
皇祖訓以厚倫有諸司職掌以立政有
punctuated:
得而舉也，政可得而齊也，禮可得而因也，道可得而乂也。故惟聖而後經天下之體立，惟明而後守天下之法融。《記》曰：「作者之謂聖，述者之謂明。」明聖者，述作之謂也。請得以是復明問焉。蓋自昔人君，定命於艱難之際，勞心於草昧之初，事熟於見聞之下，慮深於憂患之餘，其於保大定功，以為燕翼計者，蓋莫不有典章焉。顧其立國之初，萬務叢舉，事每病於不給；承平則愈復闊略，物忘其舊，率多簡陋之風。故以西漢之盛，二百年無服章之制；雖《唐六典》，亦蒙宇文之舊，徒文具而無所設施；《宋會要》不定朝會之儀，至熙寧而始議其禮。其他固不足徵也。
於惟皇祖，躬上聖之資，雄曠古之績，盡倫盡制，有綱有紀。故其見於制作也，有《皇祖訓》以厚倫，有《諸司職掌》以立政，有
translation_en:
…can be brought into effect; government can be brought into order; rites can be carried forward; and the Way can be brought into orderly operation. Thus only through sageliness can the essential framework for ordering all under Heaven be established, and only through discernment can the rules for preserving all under Heaven be fully integrated. The Record of Rites says: “One who creates is called a sage; one who transmits is called discerning.” Discernment and sageliness refer to transmission and creation. Permit me to respond to your discerning question on this basis.
From antiquity, rulers secured their mandate amid hardship and labored in mind at the unsettled beginnings of their reigns. Their familiarity with affairs grew through what they saw and heard, and their deliberations deepened through anxiety and adversity. In preserving their great achievements and consolidating their accomplishments, thereby planning for the peace and security of their descendants, they invariably established statutes and institutions. Yet at the founding of a state, myriad tasks arose together, and affairs repeatedly suffered from inadequate provision. In times of settled peace, arrangements became still more lax and cursory; institutions lost their earlier forms, and a rudimentary character generally prevailed. Thus, despite the flourishing of the Western Han, for two hundred years there was no system governing ceremonial dress and insignia. Even the Six Statutes of the Tang inherited the old arrangements of the Yuwen house: they existed merely as documentary provisions, without being put into practice. The Collected Essentials of the Song did not settle the ceremonial forms for court assemblies; only in the Xining era did deliberations on these rites begin. Other examples scarcely merit citing.
Ah, our imperial ancestor personally possessed the qualities of supreme sageliness and achieved mighty deeds unmatched in antiquity. He fulfilled human relationships and perfected institutions, establishing guiding principles and orderly rules. Thus, among the institutions and regulations he created were the Instructions of the Imperial Ancestor, to strengthen human relationships, and the Responsibilities of the Various Offices, to establish orderly government; there were also…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
洪武禮制
大明集禮
孝慈錄教民榜諸書以貞天下之教有
大誥
大明令
大明律軍法定律諸書以弼天下之教黜釐元
政弘敷
帝猷
聖王之文燦然備具所謂本道德也所謂致隆
===
高也所謂綦文理也其視禹之典則湯之
儆訓文武之謨烈不遐有光矣嗚呼盛哉
所以經天下之體也非
聖其誰能脩之
成祖紹統
列聖承休
憲章之在率履不越經理之宜潤色咸備至於
敬皇思成
太祖之志稍遵條格之規開局編摩發揚
punctuated:
《洪武禮制》、《大明集禮》、《孝慈錄》、《教民榜》諸書，以貞天下之教；有《大誥》、《大明令》、《大明律》、《軍法定律》諸書，以弼天下之教。黜釐元政，弘敷帝猷，聖王之文燦然備具。所謂本道德也，所謂致隆高也，所謂綦文理也。其視禹之典則、湯之儆訓、文武之謨烈，不遐有光矣！嗚呼，盛哉！所以經天下之體也，非聖，其誰能脩之？

成祖紹統，列聖承休，憲章之在，率履不越；經理之宜，潤色咸備。至於敬皇，思成太祖之志，稍遵條格之規，開局編摩，發揚
translation_en:
…such works as the Hongwu Ritual Regulations, the Collected Rites of the Great Ming, the Record of Filial Piety and Parental Kindness, and the Placards for Instructing the People, to set the instruction of all under Heaven on the correct course; and such works as the Grand Pronouncements, the Ordinances of the Great Ming, the Code of the Great Ming, and the Established Statutes of Military Law, to reinforce that instruction. He abolished and reformed the governmental practices of the Yuan and broadly extended the imperial designs. The cultural institutions of the sage king were splendidly complete. This is what is meant by taking morality as the foundation, by attaining the utmost sublimity, and by bringing cultural order to its fullest refinement. Compared with the statutes and standards of Yu, the admonitory teachings of Tang, and the plans and achievements of Kings Wen and Wu, did these not likewise shine across the ages? Ah, how magnificent! Such was the framework for ordering all under Heaven. Who but a sage could have fashioned it?

Chengzu succeeded to the imperial line, and the successive sage sovereigns inherited its blessings. They followed the established institutions without departing from them, and fully supplied the refinements appropriate to the ordering of affairs. When it came to Emperor Jing, he sought to fulfill Taizu’s intentions. Gradually following the prescribed regulations, he established a bureau to compile and edit, and to bring to light…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
盛典其所宗本以諸司職掌為主其所纂輯以
祖訓諸書為据以其所關之重故事雖細而必
錄以其所著之善故今雖寢而必存起於
洪武之初元附以
歷朝之行事綱領宏大類例該洽
朝家之式秩然咸在所謂總方略也所謂一
統類也所謂振毫末也將使奉法之吏誦
數之儒歸極之眾是彝是訓矣嗚呼休玆
所以守天下之法也非
===
明其孰能脩之若其於周官唐典之同異則有
可言者愚故不可以不盡也唐典姑置諸
周禮一書蓋周公旣相成王建都於洛乃
損益二代之制定為一王之法筆削旣成
不可附益雖洛邑之建必有官屬一不綴
及歸於一統耳曰孺子來相宅其大惇
典篤前人成烈是已彼所謂惇典成烈之
書也比於諸司職掌蓋庶幾焉會典者抑
蘇洵所謂纂集故事使無忘於後人如其
punctuated:
盛典。其所宗本，以《諸司職掌》為主；其所纂輯，以《祖訓》諸書為据。以其所關之重，故事雖細而必錄；以其所著之善，故今雖寢而必存。起於洪武之初元，附以歷朝之行事，綱領宏大，類例該洽，朝家之式，秩然咸在。所謂總方略也，所謂一統類也，所謂振毫末也。將使奉法之吏、誦數之儒、歸極之眾，是彝是訓矣。嗚呼，休玆！所以守天下之法也，非明其孰能脩之？
若其於《周官》、唐典之同異，則有可言者，愚故不可以不盡也。唐典姑置諸。《周禮》一書，蓋周公旣相成王，建都於洛，乃損益二代之制，定為一王之法。筆削旣成，不可附益。雖洛邑之建，必有官屬，一不綴及，歸於一統耳。曰：「孺子來相宅，其大惇典，篤前人成烈。」是已。彼所謂惇典成烈之書也，比於《諸司職掌》，蓋庶幾焉。《會典》者，抑蘇洵所謂纂集故事，使無忘於後人，如其
translation_en:
…the grand institutions. Its principal foundation was the Duties of the Various Offices (Zhusi zhizhang), and its compilation drew upon the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun) and other books. Because of the importance of the matters involved, precedents were necessarily recorded, however minute; because of the excellence they embodied, they were necessarily preserved, even if now discontinued. Beginning with the first year of Hongwu, it incorporated the practices of successive reigns. Its organizing framework was comprehensive, its categories and precedents all-embracing; the court’s regulations were all present in orderly arrangement. This is what is meant by bringing together the guiding principles, unifying the categories, and attending to the smallest details. Officials who uphold the law, scholars who recite and enumerate the texts, and the multitude who turn toward the supreme standard would thereby take these as their constant norms and instructions. Ah, how splendid! These are the means of preserving the laws of the realm. Who but an enlightened ruler could put them in order?
As for its similarities to and differences from the Offices of Zhou and the Tang compendium, there are matters to discuss, and I, in my ignorance, cannot leave them unexplained. Let us set aside the Tang compendium for the moment. The Rites of Zhou was produced after the Duke of Zhou had become chief minister to King Cheng and established the capital at Luo. He then modified the institutions of the two preceding dynasties, establishing them as the laws of a single sovereign. Once the work of composition and revision was complete, nothing further could be appended. Although the establishment of Luoyi must have entailed a complement of officials, none was added to the text: the aim was simply to preserve a unified system. The passage, “Let the young sovereign come to inspect his dwelling; let him greatly esteem the statutes and firmly uphold his predecessors’ accomplished achievements,” expresses precisely this. That work is what may be called a book for esteeming the statutes and preserving accomplished achievements. It is thus fairly close to the Duties of the Various Offices. The Collected Statutes (Huidian), on the other hand, is rather what Su Xun described as compiling precedents so that later generations would not forget them, like his…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
所編嘉祐禮書隨事記錄詳其曲折不爲
筆削者是已故不必取合乎周禮耳恭惟
皇上獨稟
神聖承運
中興
大孝
尊親
主敬法
祖議禮制度有述有作追隆古之上儀備
===
皇朝之法則郁郁乎洋洋乎體大而文洽
德昭而福應蓋愚之所不能殫舉也茲復申
命儒臣脩輯會典誠欲其官無曠牒禮無漏儀
事歸於盡善盡美者矣今者碩輔論思名
儒校理秘籍載啓嘉謨允列所以翊
右文之盛治贊不朽之大業者固非野人小
子之所得窺也而執事乃假以載筆之言
重以下風之佐惡乎其不足以承明問也
蓋愚聞之事者君子行之而小人言焉愚
punctuated:
所編嘉祐禮書，隨事記錄，詳其曲折，不爲筆削者是已。故不必取合乎周禮耳。
恭惟皇上獨稟神聖，承運中興，大孝尊親，主敬法祖，議禮制度，有述有作，追隆古之上儀，備皇朝之法則。郁郁乎！洋洋乎！體大而文洽，德昭而福應，蓋愚之所不能殫舉也。茲復申命儒臣脩輯會典，誠欲其官無曠牒，禮無漏儀，事歸於盡善盡美者矣。今者碩輔論思，名儒校理，秘籍載啓，嘉謨允列，所以翊右文之盛治、贊不朽之大業者，固非野人小子之所得窺也。而執事乃假以載筆之言，重以下風之佐，惡乎其不足以承明問也？蓋愚聞之：「事者，君子行之，而小人言焉。」愚
translation_en:
…as in the Book of Rites of the Jiayou Era (Jiayou lishu) that he compiled: matters were recorded as they arose, their particulars fully set out, without editorial selection or revision. Thus there is no need to make it conform to the Rites of Zhou.
I respectfully reflect that His Majesty alone is endowed with divine sagacity. Receiving Heaven’s mandate, he has brought about a restoration; with supreme filial devotion he honors his parents, makes reverence his guiding principle, and follows his ancestors’ example. In deliberating on rites and establishing institutions, he has both transmitted and created, emulating the highest ceremonies of remote antiquity and completing the regulations of our imperial dynasty. How richly cultivated! How magnificent! Their substance is grand and their forms comprehensive; his virtue shines forth, and blessings respond. These are more than I, in my ignorance, can enumerate exhaustively. Now he has again commanded his Confucian ministers to revise and compile the Collected Statutes (Huidian), truly wishing that no office should lack its documentary record and no rite omit any ceremonial observance, so that all affairs may attain complete excellence and perfection.
At present, eminent chief ministers deliberate and reflect, while renowned scholars collate and edit. Treasured documents are opened anew, and excellent counsels duly arrayed. How these efforts sustain a flourishing government that esteems letters and advance an imperishable undertaking is assuredly beyond the understanding of a rustic youngster such as myself. Yet you have entrusted me with a statement concerning the work of recording, and further accorded weight to the assistance I might offer from my humble position. How, then, could this fail to furnish a response to your discerning question? For I have heard it said: “As for affairs, the gentleman carries them out, while the petty man speaks of them.” I, in my ignorance …

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
也亦將有小人之言於此蓋會典以纂集
爲務故有類聚而無筆削周禮以典常爲
主故有定載而無附續故會典獨可採集
近事增續舊文所謂備所未備者也若夫
精而益精則我
皇上明聖之烈述作之宗遼廓千載此其一遇
也語曰日中必熭操刀必割謂宜折衷象
魏之書參伍
皇王之紀作爲一經傳之無窮所謂懸諸日月
===
不刊之書也不其偉歟草野之見誠不知
其可否亦惟執事有以教之
第二問
胡庭蘭
同考試官教諭江批樂導和者也不得聲氣
之元而祗以器數論樂抑末矣子於議評之間而
知歸重于心焉蓋觀樂之深者豈但竑博已耶
考試官教諭黃批考究精詳品裁允確非
剽竊者所可倫也
punctuated:
也，亦將有小人之言於此。蓋會典以纂集爲務，故有類聚而無筆削；周禮以典常爲主，故有定載而無附續。故會典獨可採集近事，增續舊文，所謂備所未備者也。若夫精而益精，則我皇上明聖之烈、述作之宗，遼廓千載，此其一遇也。語曰：「日中必熭，操刀必割。」謂宜折衷象魏之書，參伍皇王之紀，作爲一經，傳之無窮，所謂懸諸日月不刊之書也。不其偉歟？草野之見，誠不知其可否，亦惟執事有以教之。

第二問
胡庭蘭

同考試官教諭江批：「樂，導和者也。不得聲氣之元，而祗以器數論樂，抑末矣。子於議評之間，而知歸重于心焉，蓋觀樂之深者，豈但竑博已耶？」

考試官教諭黃批：「考究精詳，品裁允確，非剽竊者所可倫也。」
translation_en:
…I too shall offer here the words of a common man. The Collected Statutes (Huidian) is concerned with compilation, and thus groups material by category without editorial judgments of inclusion or exclusion. The Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) takes established institutions as its foundation, and thus has a fixed text without appended continuations. Hence the Collected Statutes alone permits the gathering of recent matters and the supplementation of earlier texts: this is what is meant by supplying what was previously lacking. As for refining it still further, the achievements of our enlightened and sagely Emperor, and his preeminence in transmitting and creating institutions, present an opportunity encountered but once across a thousand years. As the saying goes, “When the sun reaches its zenith, one must dry things in it; when one takes up a knife, one must cut.” I suggest that the writings setting forth laws at the palace gates should be critically reconciled and the records of emperors and kings compared, to produce a single canonical work transmitted for all time—a book, as the saying goes, hung beside the sun and moon, never to be altered. Would this not be magnificent? These are the views of a man from the countryside; I truly do not know whether they are acceptable, and look only to you, honored sir, for instruction.

Second Question
Hu Tinglan

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Instructor: “Music guides harmony. To discuss music solely in terms of instruments and numerical relationships, without grasping the source of sound and vital energy, is surely to concern oneself with secondary matters. In your discussion and appraisal, you know to place the emphasis on the heart. You are evidently someone with a profound understanding of music; how could your merit consist merely in breadth of learning?”

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: “The investigation is meticulous and detailed, and the appraisals sound and accurate. Those who pilfer others’ writings cannot compare with this.”

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
考試官學正林批學有根據文有條理
聖王之作樂也所以宣天地之氣而洩人
心之和者也蓋人心之和與天地之氣相
為流通故達於聲氣之元者而後可以善
音律之用通於人心之極者而後可以妙
推行之機持此以作樂則情文兼舉本末
具備可以為一代之大成矣苟弗此之務
而徒滯其迹於聲變異同之間備其數於
脩短廣狹之辨則所謂樂器之末者且未
===
之識矣其何以語作樂之大方哉此固執
事策諸生之意也請敬陳之記曰流而不
息合同而化而樂興焉言樂之所自始也
易曰雷出地奮豫先王以作樂崇德言樂
之所由作也稽昔淳古葦籥女媧笙簧伏
羲紀陽氣而為律黃帝以鳳鳴而定音樂
有由作矣是故聲出于日其法五行之說
乎如甲己為角乙庚為商之類是已五行
相滅而後相生猶五音相反而不相和也
punctuated:
考試官學正林批：學有根據，文有條理。

聖王之作樂也，所以宣天地之氣而洩人心之和者也。蓋人心之和與天地之氣相為流通，故達於聲氣之元者，而後可以善音律之用；通於人心之極者，而後可以妙推行之機。持此以作樂，則情文兼舉，本末具備，可以為一代之大成矣。苟弗此之務，而徒滯其迹於聲變異同之間，備其數於脩短廣狹之辨，則所謂樂器之末者且未之識矣，其何以語作樂之大方哉？此固執事策諸生之意也，請敬陳之。

《記》曰：「流而不息，合同而化，而樂興焉。」言樂之所自始也。《易》曰：「雷出地奮，豫。先王以作樂崇德。」言樂之所由作也。稽昔淳古葦籥，女媧笙簧，伏羲紀陽氣而為律，黃帝以鳳鳴而定音，樂有由作矣。是故聲出于日，其法五行之說乎？如甲己為角，乙庚為商之類是已。五行相滅而後相生，猶五音相反而不相和也。
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Lin, an Instructor: “His learning has a firm foundation, and his writing is well organized.”

The sage kings created music to give expression to the vital energy of Heaven and Earth and to release the harmony of the human heart. The harmony of the human heart and the vital energy of Heaven and Earth circulate through one another. Thus, only those who comprehend the source of sound and vital energy can make proper use of tones and pitch standards; only those who penetrate the ultimate reaches of the human heart can master the workings through which music is put into practice. Creating music on this basis brings feeling and formal expression into play together and encompasses both root and branches. It can therefore constitute the great consummation of an age. If one neglects this task, merely becoming mired in the similarities and differences of tonal changes and completing numerical calculations through distinctions of length and breadth, one has not even understood the subsidiary matters concerning musical instruments. How could one discuss the great principles of creating music? This, surely, is your intention in putting this policy question to us students. Allow me respectfully to set forth my answer.

The Book of Rites says: “They flow without ceasing, unite and transform, and music arises therein.” This speaks of music’s beginnings. The Book of Changes says: “Thunder emerges from the earth and stirs: Enthusiasm. The former kings accordingly created music to exalt virtue.” This speaks of the grounds on which music was created. Looking back to remote antiquity, there were reed pipes; Nüwa had reed mouth organs; Fuxi established pitch standards by ordering the yang energy; and the Yellow Emperor fixed the tones by the phoenix’s cry. Music thus had its origins. Accordingly, tones derive from the days: does this take the doctrine of the Five Phases as its model? Examples include the days designated jia and ji corresponding to the jue tone, and yi and geng to the shang tone. The Five Phases extinguish one another before generating one another [?], just as the five tones oppose one another and do not harmonize with one another [?].

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
律出于辰其法十二辰之說乎如子爲黃
鍾寅爲太簇之類是已辰固順布而不窮
猶律以旋宮而各足也要之聲出于天天
無形也律制于地地有形也有形生於無
形而無形者復資於有形聲律顧可二乎
哉自是言聲者有五聲二變有班固之七
始胡樂之七華夫婆陀般瞻音出侏儒鴃
識沙臘聲局方外斯所謂夷制也亦不足
云矣彼黃鍾林鍾太簇爲三才之始姑洗
===
===
蕤賓南呂夷則爲四時之始固亦術數之
末技制樂之餘規也可與七音同語哉吾
所取者文武之全音耳蓋曰宮曰徵曰羽
曰商曰角其相次相間犁然分矣故角徵
之間近徵也收一聲謂之變徵羽宮之間
近宮也收一聲謂之變宮何也宮爲君商
爲臣角爲民徵爲事羽爲物也臣有常職
民有常業物有常形是故角徵羽三宮所
以無變也君總萬務貴通變以宜民事屬
punctuated: 律出于辰，其法十二辰之說乎？如子爲黃鍾、寅爲太簇之類是已。辰固順布而不窮，猶律以旋宮而各足也。要之，聲出于天，天無形也；律制于地，地有形也。有形生於無形，而無形者復資於有形，聲律顧可二乎哉？自是言聲者，有五聲二變，有班固之七始、胡樂之七華。夫婆陀般瞻，音出侏儒鴃識；沙臘，聲局方外，斯所謂夷制也，亦不足云矣。彼黃鍾、林鍾、太簇爲三才之始，姑洗、蕤賓、南呂、夷則爲四時之始，固亦術數之末技、制樂之餘規也，可與七音同語哉？吾所取者，文武之全音耳。蓋曰宮、曰徵、曰羽、曰商、曰角，其相次相間，犁然分矣。故角徵之間，近徵也，收一聲謂之變徵；羽宮之間，近宮也，收一聲謂之變宮。何也？宮爲君，商爲臣，角爲民，徵爲事，羽爲物也。臣有常職，民有常業，物有常形，是故角徵羽三宮所以無變也。君總萬務，貴通變以宜民；事屬
translation_en:
…Pitch standards derive from the earthly branches: does this follow the doctrine of the twelve earthly branches? Examples are zi corresponding to Huangzhong and yin to Taicu. The branches indeed proceed in orderly succession without end, just as the pitch standards, through rotation of the modal tonic, are each complete. In essence, tones originate in Heaven, which has no form; pitch standards are established on Earth, which has form. What has form arises from the formless, while the formless in turn depends upon what has form. Can tones and pitch standards really be treated as two separate things?

Thus, those who discuss tones speak of the five tones and two altered tones, of Ban Gu’s “Seven Beginnings,” and of the “Seven Flowers” of foreign music. As for Potuobanzhan [?], its notes come from dwarfs and unintelligible, shrike-like speech [?]; Shala [?] has sounds confined to lands beyond the civilized realm. These are what are called barbarian systems and are not worth discussing. As for Huangzhong, Linzhong, and Taicu being the beginnings of the Three Powers, and Guxian, Ruibin, Nanlü, and Yize being the beginnings of the four seasons, these too are merely minor techniques of numerical arts and subsidiary rules for making music. Can they be discussed on the same footing as the seven tones? What I adopt is simply the complete tonal system of Kings Wen and Wu.

The tones called gong, zhi, yu, shang, and jue are distinctly differentiated in their succession and intervals. Thus, between jue and zhi, close to zhi, one introduces a tone called altered zhi; between yu and gong, close to gong, one introduces a tone called altered gong. Why is this? Gong represents the ruler; shang, the minister; jue, the people; zhi, affairs; and yu, material things. Ministers have constant duties, the people have constant occupations, and material things have constant forms. This is why the three tonal positions jue, zhi, and yu have no alterations [?]. The ruler oversees all affairs and values adapting to change to benefit the people; affairs pertain to …

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
萬機必化裁以盡利是故宮徵二宮所以
有變也言律者有京房之六十律有黃帝
之十二均王朴之十一均夫黃鍾仲吕固
名正聲執始南事奚取變律况包育待謙
等篇斯所稱噍殺也亦舛於樂矣彼虛宮
之位而不用其大君取足四聲而不知其
全律朴亦闇地奮之義夫殷奏之宜也豈
足云十二律之衍歟吾所取者黃帝之十
二均耳蓋十二律八十四調義取旋宮象
===
月數矣五聲之竝行以宮而爲主君子謂
成損益之規得黃鍾之正矣何也黃鍾萬
事根本作樂之元也是故其制長九寸各
因而損益之以和音樂音樂得其和是役
眾律也以正時序以審五度以嘉五量以
謹五權非他律所能役也至於正聲子聲
之別正律變律之辨其指又可知已夫正
聲十二全律也子聲十二半律也變聲又
十二變律也一均之内宮聲爲主是故商
punctuated:
萬機，必化裁以盡利，是故宮徵二宮所以有變也。

言律者，有京房之六十律，有黃帝之十二均、王朴之十一均。夫黃鍾、仲吕固名正聲，執始、南事奚取變律？况包育待謙等篇，斯所稱噍殺也，亦舛於樂矣。彼虛宮之位而不用其大君，取足四聲而不知其全律，朴亦闇地奮之義，夫殷奏之宜也，豈足云十二律之衍歟？吾所取者黃帝之十二均耳。蓋十二律八十四調，義取旋宮，象月數矣。五聲之竝行，以宮而爲主，君子謂成損益之規，得黃鍾之正矣。何也？黃鍾萬事根本，作樂之元也。是故其制長九寸，各因而損益之，以和音樂。音樂得其和，是役眾律也。以正時序，以審五度，以嘉五量，以謹五權，非他律所能役也。

至於正聲子聲之別，正律變律之辨，其指又可知已。夫正聲十二全律也，子聲十二半律也，變聲又十二變律也。一均之内，宮聲爲主，是故商
translation_en:
…the myriad affairs; adaptation and judicious adjustment are essential to realize every benefit. This is why the two notes gong and zhi have altered forms.

Among accounts of pitch standards are Jing Fang’s sixty pitch standards, the Yellow Emperor’s twelve modal systems, and Wang Pu’s eleven modal systems. Huangzhong and Zhonglü are certainly designated fundamental tones; why adopt altered pitch standards such as Zhishi and Nanshi? Moreover, such pieces as “Baoyu” and “Daiqian” [?] exemplify what is called a shrill and attenuated sound, and likewise depart from proper music. He leaves the position of gong vacant and does not employ its great ruler, regarding four notes as sufficient without understanding the complete system of pitch standards. Pu also fails to understand the meaning of [thunder] stirring from the earth and the propriety of solemn musical performance [?]. How could his system qualify as an elaboration of the twelve pitch standards? What I adopt is simply the Yellow Emperor’s twelve modal systems. The twelve pitch standards and eighty-four modes embody the principle of rotating the gong tonic, corresponding to the number of months. The five notes operate together, with gong as their ruler. The gentleman calls this the fulfillment of the rules of diminution and augmentation and the attainment of Huangzhong’s correct standard. Why? Huangzhong is the foundation of all affairs and the origin of music-making. Its prescribed pipe length is therefore nine cun; the others are each derived through diminution and augmentation, bringing music into harmony. When music attains harmony, this is Huangzhong directing all the pitch standards. It regulates the sequence of the seasons, verifies the five measures of length, makes proper the five measures of capacity, and ensures precision in the five weights. These are functions that no other pitch standard can perform.

As for the distinction between fundamental tones and subsidiary tones, and the differentiation between fundamental and altered pitch standards, their meaning can also be understood. The fundamental tones are the twelve full-length pitch pipes; the subsidiary tones are the twelve half-length pitch pipes; the altered tones are another twelve altered pitch pipes. Within a single modal system, the gong tone is the ruler. Therefore, shang…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
性命也守近易者則博識文章曰至也不知文
章乃人倫之發使道之近易而遺人倫是俗學
也非文章也故以子貢之聞性道猶言事君事
親以息倦子游以文學稱而曰灑掃應對末也
而非本彼惡知其所學正以學為事君事親以
此息倦則其所乾乾者何學也聖道更無精粗
灑掃應對精義入神一理耳而分本末兩事可
乎堯之命舜曰慎徽五典舜之命契曰敬敷五
教堯舜之道無他孝弟而已矣是故精義入神
===
精者人倫也灑掃應對粗者亦人倫也多識博
文博此人倫也盡性至命至此人倫也人曰至
人人之外無所謂至也倫曰至倫倫之外無所
謂人也人莫不飲食也鮮能知味也夫孰不為
人也而不知所以盡人耳謂之盡人人人可以
自盡天下無無人倫之人則無不可作聖之人
矣其有至不至譬之行者聖人則已適國吾或
半塗而廢然天下達道固莫得而阻之使不至
也吾惟卽人倫以作聖繇達道以脩身則是至
punctuated: 性命也。守近易者，則博識文章曰至也，不知文章乃人倫之發。使道之近易而遺人倫，是俗學也，非文章也。故以子貢之聞性道，猶言事君事親以息倦；子游以文學稱，而曰灑掃應對末也，而非本。彼惡知其所學？正以學為事君事親，以此息倦，則其所乾乾者何學也？聖道更無精粗，灑掃應對、精義入神，一理耳，而分本末兩事，可乎？堯之命舜曰：「慎徽五典。」舜之命契曰：「敬敷五教。」堯舜之道無他，孝弟而已矣。是故精義入神，精者人倫也；灑掃應對，粗者亦人倫也。多識博文，博此人倫也；盡性至命，至此人倫也。人曰至人，人之外無所謂至也；倫曰至倫，倫之外無所謂人也。人莫不飲食也，鮮能知味也。夫孰不為人也，而不知所以盡人耳。謂之盡人，人人可以自盡。天下無無人倫之人，則無不可作聖之人矣。其有至不至，譬之行者，聖人則已適國，吾或半塗而廢。然天下達道，固莫得而阻之使不至也。吾惟卽人倫以作聖，繇達道以脩身，則是至
translation_en:
…human nature and destiny. Those who hold to what is near at hand and easy regard extensive knowledge and literary accomplishment as the ultimate attainment, not knowing that literary accomplishment is the expression of human relationships. If one treats the Way as near at hand and easy yet leaves out human relationships, this is vulgar learning, not literary accomplishment. Thus even Zigong, who had heard teachings on human nature and the Way, still spoke of serving his ruler and parents as a means of resting from weariness. Ziyou was renowned for literary learning, yet said that sweeping and cleaning, responding and answering were the branches, not the root. How could they understand what they were learning? If learning consists precisely in serving one’s ruler and parents, and one seeks rest from weariness in these activities, then what learning is the object of one’s unremitting exertion? The Way of the sages admits no distinction between the refined and the coarse. Sweeping and cleaning, responding and answering, and refining one’s understanding of moral principles to penetrate the spiritual all embody a single principle. Can they be divided into two separate matters, root and branches?

Yao instructed Shun, saying, “Carefully promote harmony in the five enduring relationships.” Shun instructed Xie, saying, “Reverently disseminate the five teachings.” The Way of Yao and Shun was nothing other than filial devotion and respect for elder brothers. Thus, in refining one’s understanding of moral principles to penetrate the spiritual, what is refined is human relationships; in sweeping and cleaning, responding and answering, what is coarse is also human relationships. Acquiring wide knowledge and broad literary learning means broadening one’s understanding of these human relationships. Fully realizing one’s nature and attaining an understanding of destiny means attaining fulfillment in these human relationships. A person may be called a perfected person, but outside being human there is no so-called perfection. Relationships may be called perfected relationships, but outside relationships there is no so-called human being. Everyone eats and drinks, but few can discern the flavor. Who is not a human being? Yet people do not understand how to fulfill their humanity. What is called fulfilling one’s humanity is something everyone can fully accomplish for themselves. Since there is no person in the world without human relationships, there is no person incapable of becoming a sage.

That some attain this and others do not may be compared to travelers: the sage has already reached the destination, while I may abandon the journey halfway. Yet as for the universally accessible Way of the world, nothing can obstruct it and prevent one from arriving. If I simply become a sage through human relationships and cultivate myself by following this universal Way, then this is the ultimate…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
角徵羽四聲短於本律故用正聲焉推
蕤賓林鍾之宮長於本律故用半聲焉推
之而正律變律可識也惡得云於樂無所
相成哉蓋天統元氣無不兼聲也地統元
形無不兼律也人統大成無不兼天地也
所謂具三才之道者非歟然形聲者天地
也諧之者人也何也樂生於音音生於律
律定於尺尺成於黍制樂者所當究心矣
夫何荀勗以角律之長而制笛自黃鍾二
===
尺八寸蕤賓三尺九寸咸長短之不倫是
四角八角之數也梁武以十二律管而制
笛自黃鍾二尺八寸至應鍾三尺三寸皆
自長而漸短是十二律長短相乗之法也
要之私見制律非其元氣律不可定已杜
夔校尺長於汲冢阮咸校尺合於始平要
之異同之間滯於形器尺不可定已晉田
父之尺則加七釐梁表之尺則加二分蔡
邕之銅籥錢樂之渾儀以至後周之玉尺
punctuated:
角徵羽四聲短於本律，故用正聲焉；推蕤賓林鍾之宮，長於本律，故用半聲焉。推之而正律變律可識也，惡得云於樂無所相成哉？蓋天統元氣，無不兼聲也；地統元形，無不兼律也；人統大成，無不兼天地也。所謂具三才之道者，非歟？然形聲者天地也，諧之者人也。何也？樂生於音，音生於律，律定於尺，尺成於黍，制樂者所當究心矣。
夫何荀勗以角律之長而制笛，自黃鍾二尺八寸、蕤賓三尺九寸，咸長短之不倫，是四角八角之數也。梁武以十二律管而制笛，自黃鍾二尺八寸至應鍾三尺三寸，皆自長而漸短，是十二律長短相乗之法也。要之，私見制律，非其元氣，律不可定已。杜夔校尺長於汲冢，阮咸校尺合於始平。要之，異同之間，滯於形器，尺不可定已。晉田父之尺則加七釐，梁表之尺則加二分。蔡邕之銅籥、錢樂之渾儀，以至後周之玉尺
translation_en:
…The four tones [?] jiao, zhi, and yu are shorter than their fundamental pitch standards, and therefore use the full-length tones. Extending this reasoning to the gong pitches of Ruibin and Linzhong, these are longer than their fundamental pitch standards, and therefore use the half-length tones. By pursuing this reasoning, one can understand the regular and altered pitch standards. How could one say that they do not complement one another in music? Heaven encompasses primordial vital energy and thus includes every sound; earth encompasses primordial form and thus includes every pitch standard; humanity encompasses their complete realization and thus includes both heaven and earth. Is this not what is meant by embodying the Way of the Three Powers? Yet heaven and earth supply form and sound; humanity brings them into harmony. Why is this? Music arises from tones, tones arise from pitch standards, pitch standards are determined by the measuring foot, and the measuring foot is established through millet grains. Those who devise music should investigate this thoroughly.
Why, then, did Xun Xu make flutes using the length of the jiao pitch standard, ranging from two chi and eight cun for Huangzhong to three chi and nine cun for Ruibin, with lengths all out of proportion? These are the numerical measures of “four jiao” and “eight jiao” [?]. Emperor Wu of Liang made flutes using the twelve pitch pipes, ranging from two chi and eight cun for Huangzhong to three chi and three cun for Yingzhong, all becoming progressively shorter [?]. This is the method of multiplying the lengths of the twelve pitch standards by one another. In sum, if pitch standards are devised from private opinion rather than grounded in primordial vital energy, they cannot be fixed.
The measuring foot calibrated by Du Kui was longer than that from the Ji Tomb, while the one calibrated by Ruan Xian matched that from Shiping. In sum, amid such agreements and discrepancies, attachment to material forms and instruments makes it impossible to fix the measuring foot. The measuring foot of the old farmer of the Jin dynasty added seven li; that of the Liang biao [?] added two fen. Cai Yong’s bronze flute, Qian Le’s [?] armillary sphere, and even the jade measuring foot of the Later Zhou…

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
鐵尺皆長二分有奇其於長短固古今異
也公孫崇以為累黍之長劉芳以為累黍
之廣元正以為取二黍之間以至李照之
以横累寸胡瑗之以横累尺其云廣狹亦
人人殊也豈非黍有大小年有豐歉歟以
黍定尺又不可成已夫古人因黍起數積
而至於度量權衡此樂之由制也後世之
黍未必如古又不求諸自悟之心乃區區
於大小廣狹之迹多見其惑矣司馬遷曰
===
樂所以為治而和正心也故宮動脾而和
正聖商動肺而和正義角動肝而和正仁
徵動心而和正禮羽動腎而和正心是樂
非自外作也故欲求音樂者亦惟求諸其
心而已矣又何必屑屑於器數清濁之間
哉後世若儒者之論樂莫備於蔡元定律
呂一編蓋其明白淵深縝密通暢九分一
寸之說則淮南大史可推五聲二變之數
則杜預通典可考黃鍾圍徑本於漢斛之
punctuated: 鐵尺，皆長二分有奇，其於長短，固古今異也。公孫崇以為累黍之長，劉芳以為累黍之廣，元正以為取二黍之間，以至李照之以横累寸、胡瑗之以横累尺，其云廣狹，亦人人殊也。豈非黍有大小，年有豐歉歟？以黍定尺，又不可成已。夫古人因黍起數，積而至於度量權衡，此樂之由制也。後世之黍未必如古，又不求諸自悟之心，乃區區於大小廣狹之迹，多見其惑矣。司馬遷曰：「樂所以為治而和正心也。故宮動脾而和正聖，商動肺而和正義，角動肝而和正仁，徵動心而和正禮，羽動腎而和正心。」是樂非自外作也。故欲求音樂者，亦惟求諸其心而已矣，又何必屑屑於器數清濁之間哉？後世若儒者之論樂，莫備於蔡元定《律呂》一編。蓋其明白淵深，縝密通暢。九分一寸之說，則《淮南》《大史》可推；五聲二變之數，則杜預《通典》可考；黃鍾圍徑，本於漢斛之
translation_en:
…and iron rulers were all longer by two fen and a fraction: the lengths certainly differed between antiquity and later times. Gongsun Chong held that millet grains should be aligned lengthwise; Liu Fang held that they should be aligned breadthwise; Yuan Zheng held that one should take the interval between two grains [?]. Then there were Li Zhao, who laid grains crosswise to establish the cun, and Hu Yuan, who laid them crosswise to establish the chi. Their accounts of breadth and narrowness likewise differed from person to person. Was this not because millet grains differ in size, and years bring abundant or poor harvests? Establishing the chi by millet grains is therefore also impracticable. The ancients began their reckoning with millet grains and, by accumulation, arrived at measures of length, capacity, and weight. This was the basis for establishing music. The millet of later ages is not necessarily like that of antiquity. Yet people do not seek understanding in their own minds, but fuss over outward particulars of size and breadth. All one sees is their confusion.

Sima Qian said: “Music is the means of bringing about good government and harmonizing and rectifying the mind. Thus the gong note stirs the spleen and harmonizes and rectifies sageliness [?]; shang stirs the lungs and harmonizes and rectifies righteousness; jue stirs the liver and harmonizes and rectifies benevolence; zhi stirs the heart and harmonizes and rectifies ritual propriety; yu stirs the kidneys and harmonizes and rectifies the mind.” Thus music does not arise from outside oneself. Those who wish to understand music need only seek it in their own minds. Why must they fuss over instruments, numerical relations, and high and low pitches?

Among later Confucian scholars’ discussions of music, none is more comprehensive than Cai Yuanding’s work Pitch Standards (Lülü). It is clear and profound, meticulous and lucid. The doctrine that nine fen make one cun can be traced through the Huainanzi and the Grand Historian’s Records [?]; the numerical relations of the five notes and two altered notes can be examined in Du Yu’s Comprehensive Institutions [?]; the circumference and diameter of the Huangzhong pitch pipe are based on the Han hu capacity measure’s …

title: 嘉靖二十八年廣東鄉試錄
text:
穗兮變徵非調出於孔氏之禮疏而先求
聲氣之元因律以生尺尤所謂卓然者然
則備音樂之缺者舍此其誰乎方今
聖天子履中樂和凝道器於一身明天察地貫
性命而成則其於制作之妙固已兼統而
會萃之矣愚也何幸躬逢其盛
第三問
謝應垣
同考試官教諭張批古者射以觀德非爲文
具是作得其體要且能敷揚我
聖祖置圃學宮育德造士至意其欲因文務實尤有真見錄之
同考試官教諭程批古今射法鋪敘殆盡而
反已自脩之意隱然自寓有志之士也
考試官教諭黃批深得立射本意
考試官學正林批條答詳盡
===
文者有其實者也禮者適於宜者也實不
足以振民育德而爛然於器數儀典之間
雖盛亦靡宜不足以興治化風而戋然於
punctuated:
穗兮，變徵非調出於孔氏之禮疏，而先求聲氣之元，因律以生尺，尤所謂卓然者。然則備音樂之缺者，舍此其誰乎？方今聖天子履中樂和，凝道器於一身，明天察地，貫性命而成則，其於制作之妙，固已兼統而會萃之矣。愚也何幸，躬逢其盛！

第三問
謝應垣

同考試官教諭張批：古者射以觀德，非爲文具。是作得其體要，且能敷揚我聖祖置圃學宮、育德造士至意。其欲因文務實，尤有真見，錄之。

同考試官教諭程批：古今射法鋪敘殆盡，而反已自脩之意隱然自寓，有志之士也。

考試官教諭黃批：深得立射本意。

考試官學正林批：條答詳盡。

translation_en:
…the grain ear [?]. The claim that the altered zhi note does not constitute a mode comes from Master Kong’s commentary on the rites. But seeking first the source of sound and vital breath, and deriving the foot measure from the pitch standards, are especially outstanding achievements. Who else, then, could remedy the deficiencies in music but this author? Now our sagely Son of Heaven abides in centrality and delights in harmony, uniting the Way and its concrete embodiments in his own person. He understands Heaven and examines Earth, comprehending human nature and destiny to establish standards. He has surely already brought together and comprehensively mastered the subtleties of creating institutions. How fortunate I, in my ignorance, am to witness this flourishing age in person!

Third Policy Question
Xie Yingyuan

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: In antiquity, archery served to reveal virtue; it was no mere formality. This composition grasps its essential principles and also expounds our sagely founding emperor’s profound intention in establishing archery grounds at the schools to nurture virtue and cultivate scholars. Its wish to pursue substance through outward forms shows particularly sound insight. Selected for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cheng, Instructor: The exposition of ancient and modern archery methods is nearly exhaustive, while the intention to examine oneself and cultivate one’s character is subtly embedded throughout. This is a scholar with aspiration.

Comment by Examiner Huang, Instructor: It profoundly grasps the original intention behind the institution of archery.

Comment by Examiner Lin, School Instructor: The answers to the individual points are detailed and exhaustive.
